# Development revisions

Revisions group iterations; each iteration groups related topics for review: corrections, improvements, capabilities or
investigations.

## Folder structure

- `README.md`: this guide.
- `NNN/README.md`: revision starting point, renderer identities and iteration index with brief outcomes or status.
- `NNN/NN-topic.md`: iteration design and decision note; for example, `001/02-light-continuity.md` is iteration 001.02.

## Iteration documents

Write a design and decision note, grouping topics by a shared goal, model or invariant rather than by glyph or work
step:

- **Title and introduction:** motivation and adopted approach.
- **Foundation and invariant:** shared sources and preserved relationships. Follow the
  [evaluation rules](../evaluation.md); label project hypotheses. Put distinct foundations beside their topics.
- **Topics:** one subsection per topic, numbered when useful, explaining the logic change and rationale. Retain rejected
  alternatives only when they explain a decision or constraint.
- **Scope and limits:** applicability, accepted review scope, limitations and unresolved work or assigned follow-up.
  Keep essential assessment evidence beside the relevant topic or limitation.

Describe the resulting behavior, not its implementation, testing or publication history. Replace superseded proposals;
omit file maps, handoffs, command/build logs, verification ledgers and artifact metadata. Keep detailed diagnostics
elsewhere. Avoid repeated status, unchanged-state reminders and document-routing prose; unchanged behavior matters only
as an invariant or scope boundary.

## Documentation ownership

The revision index owns lifecycle status, closure dates and renderer identities; iteration notes own model decisions and
scoped assessment. Evaluation principles belong in the [evaluation guide](../evaluation.md); commands, APIs and
interface contracts belong in tool documentation. Preview selections belong in configuration and policy files. Link to
the owner rather than repeat its content. Vendored baseline/candidate documentation remains independent.

## Iteration lifecycle

Feedback may extend an iteration's agreed topics. Close only with explicit user agreement and a disposition for each:
completed, accepted with limits, declined or deferred to a specific follow-up. Passing tests, publishing a preview or
completing one topic does not close the group. Advance numbering after closure, with the next scope agreed from
feedback.

This interface covers native generation, renderer selection and layout consumed by the WASM and specimen adapters.
[Setup, commands and settings defaults](README.md) are separate from the [published specimen contract](CONTRACT.md).
Renderer identities and model decisions belong to the [revision index](../../docs/revisions/001/README.md#iterations).

## Supported input and output

Input is one sfnt TTF/OTF with glyf, CFF or CFF2 outlines, fixed or variable. Collections, WOFF/WOFF2, bitmap-only and
color fonts require a separate adapter or conversion. Axis tags and values are checked against the font; omitted axes
use its defaults. Missing glyphs either fail or are listed as skipped, according to settings.

The repertoire supports Latin, Greek, Cyrillic and common symbols. Combining marks, control/format characters and other
scripts fail with unsupported-shaping errors. HarfRust resolves each isolated scalar at the requested axes. One-to-one
substitutions, including
[required variation alternates](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/typography/opentype/spec/features_pt#tag-rvrn), select
the glyph used for outlines, geometry, advances and kerning. `codepoint` retains Unicode identity; `glyph_id` records
the glyph drawn and can differ from the nominal character map.

Optional ligatures/contextual alternates are disabled. Each scalar must produce exactly one non-missing glyph without
positioning. Offsets, vertical advances and standalone horizontal advance adjustments fail; the latter are checked
against the shaper's own metric before positioning or pixel rounding, preserving fractional linear source metrics. Pairs
must preserve the isolated glyph IDs, order and count; only a left-advance adjustment is representable.
Context-dependent substitutions, offsets and right-advance changes fail. Complete text-run shaping requires a separate
adapter.

`generate(font_bytes, &Config)` returns sorted glyphs, skipped codepoints, sorted nonzero kerning pairs and line
metrics. Pixels are row-major **unpacked** levels from zero (no ink) to `2^output_bits - 1` (full ink). `left` and `top`
locate the bitmap relative to a baseline in y-down coordinates; empty glyphs retain advances. Advances, pair
adjustments, ascent, descent and line gap use signed 26.6 pixels (divide by 64). Ascent/descent retain font signs,
conventionally positive ascent and negative descent; line spacing is ascent minus descent plus line gap. Add pair
adjustments to the left advance.

Outlines are hinted as requested; `generate` uses variation-aware linear advances with explicit output rounding.
Consumers place origins on the pixel grid; fractional-origin rasterization and LVGL packing are outside this interface.

With the `candidate` feature, `candidate::generate_bitmap_font(font_bytes, &Config, strategy)` exports 1-bit or 3-bit
strikes with candidate bitmaps/offsets, whole-pixel advances and sparse whole-pixel pair adjustments. Other depths fail.
The `*_26_6` fields still encode pixels in multiples of 64. Consumers accumulate these metrics according to the
[spacing contract](#live-spacing-api); the optional strategy affects Mono and is ignored for Gray strikes.
`candidate::generate_bitmap_font_with_tracking(font_bytes, &Config, strategy, letter_spacing_px)` bakes uniform tracking
into those advances; bitmaps, offsets and pair adjustments remain unchanged.

## Playdate font export

`playdate::export(font_bytes, &ExportRequest)` returns a standalone UTF-8 `.fnt` with an embedded PNG image table, glyph
widths and sparse signed pair adjustments, following the
[Playdate source-font format](https://sdk.play.date/Inside%20Playdate.html#_fonts). `ExportRequest` contains `config:
Config`, `pipeline: RenderPipeline` and `letter_spacing_px` (default zero). The candidate feature and 1-bit output are
required. The selected stages, axes, repertoire, scan settings, kerning and uniform tracking produce the same finalized
bitmap metrics as explicit-pipeline preview. Tracking is already included in advances; the consumer must not add it
again. `playdate::encode(&GeneratedFont)` serializes an existing finalized strike without refitting or rounding its
metrics.

The supported export subset has 1–1024 distinct characters within U+0020–U+3FFFF, excluding controls and unsupported
shaping. Missing glyphs fail even with `missing_glyphs: "skip"`. Dimensions and advances are limited to 255 pixels;
advances must be nonnegative integers and pair adjustments must be integers within -128–127 pixels. Cells share the
preview baseline and line height. Every cell shifts right by a common inset covering the leftmost actual ink across the
export, following [pdfontconv](https://github.com/ttencate/pdfontconv/blob/main/main.js); the inset folds into shared
tracking so each pen advance and interglyph step is unchanged. Playdate-reported text bounds include the terminal cell
padding after the final glyph, so measured widths exceed the source advance sums by that padding. Transparent scanner
padding imposes no ink bounds; only actual ink constrains the inset. Ink outside the line cell vertically fails with the
codepoint rather than being clipped or shifted. The image table is limited to 16,777,216 pixels.

Widths plus shared tracking reproduce finalized advances; shared tracking can be negative to retain the common left
inset and right overhangs. Pair adjustments are unchanged. An informational `--origin_x` header records the inset and is
ignored by Playdate; it is omitted when zero so those outputs stay byte-identical. Glyph entries precede pair entries
and use explicit Unicode names. Glyphs and pairs are ordered by codepoint. For equal inputs and implementation, native
and WASM exports are byte-identical. Invalid or unrepresentable data returns an error without a partial font.

## Renderer routing

`generate` uses the separate `vendor/skrifa-baseline` snapshot for automatic Mono fitting. Independent reference capture
uses registry Skrifa. The optional `candidate` feature exposes registry-backed fitting; disabling it leaves production
on the baseline. Versions are metadata, not per-iteration Cargo features. `iteration` remains a compatibility alias for
`candidate`, not a production renderer selector.

For production `auto_fallback`, embedded interpretation remains embedded and selected automatic Mono uses the legacy
custom policy. Explicit `interpreter` and `none` preserve those paths. Gray production uses symmetric Normal rendering
with linear metric preservation. The [baseline patch policy](vendor/skrifa-baseline/PATCH.md) owns its maintenance
rules.

### Working candidate fitting

`surface::PreparedFont::new(Vec<u8>)` owns immutable font bytes. Its `render_text_with_fitting_strategy` and
`render_text_with_pipeline_and_spacing` methods accept the same request, selection and tracking arguments as the
corresponding raw-byte functions, with identical validation and output. `as_bytes()` provides read-only access; there is
no byte-replacement operation. Reuse must preserve validation and output independently of preceding requests, eviction
and the lifetime of other prepared fonts. Raw-byte entry points retain identical output without shared cache state.

Current native preview clients use `surface::render_text_with_pipeline(font_bytes, &TextRenderRequest, RenderPipeline)`.
`RenderPipeline` separates `fitting` (`font_hints_auto`, `font_hints_first`, `source_relative` or `upstream_mono`) from
`rasterization` (`free_type_mono`, `free_type_mono_terminals` or `coverage`). It requires the `candidate` feature.
Optional `diagonal_fitting` defaults to `false`; `true` requires 1-bit FreeType scan conversion with `font_hints_auto`
or `upstream_mono`. Its fixed donor reference is independent of the requested text. Unsupported geometry retains the
preceding fitted outline. The [fitting sequence](../../docs/hobby-fitting.md#approved-fitting-sequence-adoption) and its
[coupled extension](../../docs/hobby-fitting.md#coupled-whole-outline-widths) own the model and gates. Modified captures
identify `diagonal-shape-05` and retain the original upstream outline, donor reference and unrounded feature source for
independent replay; the preference does not change metrics or layout. Fitting owns engine selection and returned
advances; rasterization consumes the fitted outline without changing geometry or metrics. The automatic fitter's
returned metrics, advances an…5459 tokens truncated…or increased ink and red `#e02020` for
decreased ink; unchanged pixels retain their shade.

Each manifest carries a `statistics` array with one record per profile: `profile`, `same_symbols`, `changed_symbols`,
`average_changed_pixels`, and `median_changed_pixels`. Each drawable character counts once per family/size/profile,
including identical glyphs omitted from image records; a changed pixel is an aligned native pixel whose quantized value
differs, and averages/medians over changed symbols are zero when none changed. Missing glyphs, cases, inputs, or render
reports fail publication with identifying details and leave the existing comparison index unchanged.

## Publication checks

Publishing guarantees: schema versions, pointer/package identity, safe variant IDs, and SHA-256 values agree; family
identities, resolved axes, size groups, and item IDs are unique and complete against the resolved configuration; profile
references and outcome-specific fields are valid; assets exist with matching hashes, native dimensions, and pixel
levels; and every relative path resolves within its package, including through symlinks. A complete, validated package
is published before any pointer or index update; each update is atomic.

/// Hobby (17) angular/width coupling weight; the printed 9 is radians.
fn width_weight(w1: f64, w2: f64, t1: [f64; 2], t2: [f64; 2], height: f64) -> f64 {
    let cos = ((t1[0] * t2[0] + t1[1] * t2[1]) / (t1[0].hypot(t1[1]) * t2[0].hypot(t2[1])))
        .clamp(-1.0, 1.0);
    let angle = cos.acos();
    let dw = (w1 - w2) / 0.7;
    500.0 / (height * height) * (-(dw * dw) - (angle / 9.0).powi(2)).exp()
}

#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
enum RowGroup {
    Position,
    Stretch,
    Bend,
    InkMatch,
}

/// Linear weighted residuals in displacements at nominal scale.
struct System {
    points: Vec<[f64; 2]>,
    height: f64,
    rows: Vec<(RowGroup, Vec<f64>, f64)>,
}

impl System {
    fn new(points: Vec<[f64; 2]>, height: f64) -> Self {
        System {
            points,
            height,
            rows: Vec::new(),
        }
    }

    /// Outer product of the correspondence basis with a direction, raveled
    /// per-coordinate `(x0, y0, x1, y1, ...)`.
    fn projected(&self, a: &Sample, dir: [f64; 2], b: Option<&Sample>) -> Vec<f64> {
        let ba = basis_row(&a.terms, self.points.len());
        let mut row = vec![0.0; 2 * self.points.len()];
        for (k, w) in ba.iter().enumerate() {
            row[2 * k] = w * dir[0];
            row[2 * k + 1] = w * dir[1];
        }
        if let Some(other) = b {
            let bb = basis_row(&other.terms, self.points.len());
            for (k, w) in bb.iter().enumerate() {
                row[2 * k] -= w * dir[0];
                row[2 * k + 1] -= w * dir[1];
            }
        }
        row
    }

    /// Hobby (1)-(3), with directions/lengths from input geometry.
    fn edge(&mut self, i: usize, j: usize) -> Result<(), ()> {
        let a = Sample::vertex(i);
        let b = Sample::vertex(j);
        let pa = a.point(&self.points);
        let pb = b.point(&self.points);
        let delta = [pb[0] - pa[0], pb[1] - pa[1]];
        let length = delta[0].hypot(delta[1]);
        if !(length > 0.0) {
            return Err(());
        }
        let tangent = [delta[0] / length, delta[1] / length];
        let normal = [-tangent[1], tangent[0]];
        let alpha1 = 1000.0 / self.height.powi(3);
        let ri = self.projected(&a, normal, None);
        let rj = self.projected(&b, normal, None);
        let sum: Vec<f64> = ri
            .iter()
            .zip(rj.iter())
            .map(|(x, y)| (x + y) * (alpha1 * length / 4.0).sqrt())
            .collect();
        let diff: Vec<f64> = rj
            .iter()
            .zip(ri.iter())
            .map(|(x, y)| (x - y) * (alpha1 * length / 12.0).sqrt())
            .collect();
        self.rows.push((RowGroup::Position, sum, 0.0));
        self.rows.push((RowGroup::Position, diff, 0.0));
        let scale = (25.0 * length / self.height).sqrt() / length;
        let stretch: Vec<f64> = self
            .projected(&b, tangent, Some(&a))
            .iter()
            .map(|x| x * scale)
            .collect();
        let bend: Vec<f64> = rj
            .iter()
            .zip(ri.iter())
            .map(|(x, y)| (x - y) * scale)
            .collect();
        self.rows.push((RowGroup::Stretch, stretch, 0.0));
        self.rows.push((RowGroup::Bend, bend, 0.0));
        Ok(())
    }

    /// Hobby (4),(5): input contacts, medial point and arc-length weight.
    fn pair(
        &self,
        a: &Sample,
        b: &Sample,
        arc: f64,
        medial: [f64; 2],
    ) -> Result<(Vec<f64>, f64, [f64; 2]), ()> {
        if !(arc.is_finite() && arc > 0.0) {
            return Err(());
        }
        let pa = a.point(&self.points);
        let pb = b.point(&self.points);
        let chord = [pa[0] - pb[0], pa[1] - pb[1]];
        let distance = chord[0].hypot(chord[1]);
        if !(distance > 0.0) {
            return Err(());
        }
        let width = 2.0 * (pa[0] - medial[0]).hypot(pa[1] - medial[1]);
        let other = 2.0 * (pb[0] - medial[0]).hypot(pb[1] - medial[1]);
        if !(width > 0.0) || (width - other).abs() > 1e-12 + 1e-10 * other.abs() {
            return Err(());
        }
        let normal = [chord[0] / distance, chord[1] / distance];
        let tangent = [-normal[1], normal[0]];
        let mut error = self.projected(a, normal, Some(b));
        for x in error.iter_mut() {
            *x /= -width;
        }
        Ok((error, width, tangent))
    }
}

/// Minimum-norm least squares via SVD, NumPy `lstsq(rcond=None)` semantics.
///
/// Rank rule matches the prototype exactly: singular values above
/// `eps * max(m, n) * sigma_max` are kept (`eps` is machine epsilon);
/// the solution is the minimum-norm one in the free modes. No regularizer,
/// no rank-loss rejection: rank deficiency still solves.
fn min_norm_solve(
    a: &nalgebra::DMatrix<f64>,
    b: &nalgebra::DVector<f64>,
) -> nalgebra::DVector<f64> {
    let (m, n) = (a.nrows(), a.ncols());
    if m == 0 || n == 0 {
        return nalgebra::DVector::zeros(n);
    }
    let svd = a.clone().svd(true, true);
    let sigmax = svd.singular_values.iter().cloned().fold(0.0_f64, f64::max);
    if !(sigmax > 0.0) {
        return nalgebra::DVector::zeros(n);
    }
    let tol = f64::EPSILON * (m.max(n) as f64) * sigmax;
    let (Some(u), Some(vt)) = (svd.u, svd.v_t) else {
        return nalgebra::DVector::zeros(n);
    };
    let utb: nalgebra::DVector<f64> = u.transpose() * b;
    let mut x = nalgebra::DVector::zeros(n);
    for (i, &s) in svd.singular_values.iter().enumerate() {
        if s > tol {
            let c = utb[i] / s;
            for j in 0..n {
                x[j] += vt[(i, j)] * c;
            }
        }
    }
    x
}

/// Per-coordinate fixed-column elimination (`System.solve` form).
fn eliminate(
    rows: &[(RowGroup, Vec<f64>, f64)],
    fixed: &HashMap<(usize, usize), f64>,
    nvars: usize,
) -> (Vec<Vec<f64>>, Vec<f64>, Vec<usize>) {
    let mut free = Vec::new();
    for v in 0..nvars {
        for c in 0..2 {
            if !fixed.contains_key(&(v, c)) {
                free.push(2 * v + c);
            }
        }
    }
    let mut matrix = Vec::with_capacity(rows.len());
    let mut constants = Vec::with_capacity(rows.len());
    // Deterministic accumulation order: HashMap iteration is random, and
    // float addition is not associative.
    let mut keys: Vec<(usize, usize)> = fixed.keys().copied().collect();
    keys.sort();
    for (_, row, constant) in rows {
        let mut adjusted = *constant;
        for &(v, c) in &keys {
            adjusted += row[2 * v + c] * fixed[&(v, c)];
        }
        matrix.push(row.clone());
        constants.push(adjusted);
    }
    (matrix, constants, free)
}

fn solve_constrained(
    rows: &[(RowGroup, Vec<f64>, f64)],
    fixed: &HashMap<(usize, usize), f64>,
    nvars: usize,

# Focused fitting audit

<!-- cspell:words CSTR Hobby's NumPy KaTeX mathcal -->

This audit covers the fitting algebra in §§2–4 and §6, including §3.1 dependencies. A checked transcription means the
symbols match the source, not that every printed expression is mathematically correct or suitable for our raster. The
[research prototype](../../../../experiments/hobby_fitting/README.md) exercises a limited subset with supplied
correspondences.

## Sources and versions

The unchanged [stored CSTR report](paper.pdf) has SHA-256
`c97bd9a7bcebfeda5ea3d62bce266372f59fbc3c466239e222cf9b8c2465ff87`. Its equation labels are used throughout this audit.
PDF page numbers are one greater than printed body pages. Strict patches in
[review.json](../../../../tools/paper_extract/review.json) reproduce the checked transcription.

The [author-hosted report](https://9p.io/who/hobby/89_2-17.pdf), linked from the author's
[publication list](https://9p.io/who/hobby/pubs.html), was downloaded unchanged on 2026-10-15 as
[author-report.pdf](author-report.pdf). SHA-256: `ed617671e7fe98dca882f4d9e83d543c0853380c07f0ed0a3822db74dd21b4df`. It
also has 43 pages, with different typesetting, equation numbering and some mathematical changes. It is not established
to be the final 47-page journal publication. The [licensing record](LICENSE.txt) applies to both copies. Only the
passages identified below were compared between versions; neither chronology nor blanket superiority of one version is
inferred.

## Equation verification

Every numbered body listed here was visually checked, including signs, bars, subscripts, radical extents and constants.
Unnumbered definitions needed to interpret them were checked too. Selected inline definitions and weights were restored;
the complete prose remains only partially proofread. Section 5 is outside this fitting audit except the coefficient
count discussed below.

| Stored equation | PDF page | Checked relationship and qualification                                                                                                                                                                     |
| --------------- | -------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| (1)             | 9–10     | Original, scaled and adjusted positions; signed endpoint normal displacements, edge length and exact integrated square. $\alpha_1\approx1000/H^3$.                                                         |
| (2)             | 10       | Tangential component of edge displacement difference divided by original length. $\alpha_2\approx25/H$.                                                                                                    |
| (3)             | 11       | Corresponding normal component; original direction fixed. $\alpha_3\approx25/H$.                                                                                                                           |
| (4)             | 14       | Twice the medial radius, not generally the chord length between the two contact points.                                                                                                                    |
| (5)             | 14       | Signed projected relative width error. $d_{AB}=(A-B)/\|A-B\|$, despite the preceding prose saying “from A to B”; $\alpha_4\approx50/H$.                                                                    |
| (6)             | 15       | Integer adjustment at an important vertical; scaled-coordinate offsets retain the chosen endpoint relation. $\beta_1\approx10^8/H^2$.                                                                      |
| (7)             | 15       | Mean/difference displacement measures normalized by total region arc length; horizontal counterpart swaps coordinates.                                                                                     |
| (8)             | 16       | Sharp-extremum phase penalty with $2.5\Delta x-\Delta y$ under the radical. Applies only in its nonnegative domain, with $\Delta x>0$; $\beta_2\approx5\times10^7/H^2$.                                    |
| (9)             | 16       | Two pixel-center relations, indexed $I_k,I_{k+1}$; $\beta_3\approx10^8/H^2$, $\max(\lvert a\rvert,\lvert b\rvert)=1/2$.                                                                                    |
| (10)            | 17–18    | Direction range bounded by $\gamma_1/w_{\max}$ and width range by $\gamma_2/\sqrt{w_{\max}}$, $\gamma_1\approx\gamma_2\approx0.25$. Direction is in radians.                                               |
| (11)            | 20       | Projected signed integer-offset residual; both integer components enter with plus signs. $\beta_4\approx2\times10^8/H^3$.                                                                                  |
| (12)            | 20       | Direction-lock residual uses $(Y_B-Y_A,X_A-X_B)$; $\beta_5\approx2\times10^6/H^3$.                                                                                                                         |
| (13)            | 21       | Offset perpendicularity uses $(I_{k+1},-I_k)/w_P^2$; $\alpha_5\approx20/H$.                                                                                                                                |
| (14)            | 21       | Reflection $(2x_B-x,y)$; horizontal and shift alternatives are described in prose.                                                                                                                         |
| (15)            | 22       | Adjustable reflection $(F_k-x,y)$ and translation-free linear part $\mathcal M_v$.                                                                                                                         |
| (16)            | 22–23    | Integrated squared symmetry displacement uses $d_{ab}=\|D\|/2$, $\alpha_6\approx5\times10^5/H^3$. Its preceding displacement definitions differ between versions; see below.                               |
| (17)            | 23       | Couples **relative errors** $E(P_i)-E(P_j)$ with $\sqrt{s_i s_j\psi_1}$. Does not demand identical widths from intentionally different source strokes.                                                     |
| (18)            | 24       | Nearby integer-adjustment X positions preserve their source difference.                                                                                                                                    |
| (19)            | 24       | Y counterpart; displacement is outside the radical. $\psi_2(x)=100H^{-2}\exp[-(x/(0.03H))^2]$.                                                                                                             |
| (20)            | 24–25    | Five integer/font-wide parameter relations and their solved substitutions.                                                                                                                                 |
| (21)            | 25–26    | Pairwise font-wide parameter differences and both displayed $\psi_3$ alternatives. Their left sides use subscripts 1/2 while the right sides use i/j, as printed; this is an index-notation inconsistency. |
| (22)            | 29–30    | Width/direction mapping and $\gamma_1/3$ by $\gamma_2/3$ buckets. Its preceding derivative differs between copies.                                                                                         |
| (31)            | 39       | Cubic Bernstein basis, control indices $3i$ through $3i+3$.                                                                                                                                                |
| (32)            | 40       | Midpoint quadrature $t=(j+1/2)/k_i$, distinct from the earlier one-third correspondence example.                                                                                                           |
| (33)            | 40–41    | Signed normal displacement times $\sqrt{\alpha_1 s_{ij}}$; unit normal $(v,-u)/\sqrt{u^2+v^2}$. Normals and arc lengths must be fixed coefficients for linear least squares.                               |

Section 2's integer-offset discussion explicitly assumes turning on pixels whose **centers** are inside the outline. Its
pixel-density claim cites Hobby's earlier work [8,9]; this audit does not re-prove that theorem or extend it to coverage
conversion. Section 4.1's height interval, weights and stopping symbols were checked against pages 26–29;
$\gamma_3\approx0.5/\sigma_{\rm hi}$, $\gamma_4\approx10$, $\gamma_5=0.65$. These are suggested heuristics, not a
complete feature classifier specification.

## Source discrepancies and interpretation

### Symmetry normal: supported alternative in the author copy

Stored page 22 defines the mean direction $D$ along matching segments, but its two displacement numerators use $D\cdot$
the positional mismatch. That measures tangential sliding rather than normal separation. The author copy, page 22,
explicitly uses $(D_y,-D_x)\cdot$ the mismatch for both endpoints (its subsequent equation is (15)). This agrees with
the normal-component construction in §3.1 and the curved symmetry expression on stored page 41. The stored transcription
retains $D\cdot$ faithfully; use the author-supported rotated normal when implementing this relationship. Reject a
zero-length mean direction rather than divide by zero. Symmetry fitting is outside the first prototype.

### Width mapping derivative: supported alternative in the author copy

Stored page 29 prints $\partial v/\partial w=\sqrt\theta$. Its own (22), $v=\frac23 w^{3/2}$, differentiates to
$\sqrt w$. The author copy, page 29, explicitly prints $\sqrt w$ before its (21). This also gives
$\Delta v\approx\sqrt w\,(\gamma_2/\sqrt w)=\gamma_2$, the stated local bucket correspondence. The stored transcription
retains $\sqrt\theta$; an implementation should use the verified mapping and its derivative. The mapping is only
approximate for finite rectangles: $u$ depends on $w$ as well as $\theta$.

### Width matching weight: surprising, but faithfully printed

Both copies, PDF page 23, print

$$\psi_1=\frac{500}{H^2}\exp\left[-\left(\frac{w_1-w_2}{0.7}\right)^2-\left(\frac{\Delta\theta}{9}\right)^2\right]$$

and explicitly say radians. No source here supports replacing 9 by degrees or another constant. At $\pi/2$ the
orientation factor is approximately 0.970, so this is a weak directional preference. The prototype keeps the printed
constant and reports this consequence. The 0.7 width scale also needs an explicit unit convention: unlike $H$-normalized
terms, it does not automatically rescale when input coordinate units change. The prototype uses pixel units and exposes
that width scale, without tuning it to glyph pixels.

### Curves: correspondence, fixed coefficients and a coordinate inconsistency

Stored page 40 and author page 40 both use **one third** as an example of mapping a point on a polygon segment to the
same fraction of its curve-parameter interval. This is correct and separate from the **midpoint** rule (32). For $k_i$
intervals the prototype uses $j=0,\ldots,k_i-1$.

The prose calls $(u_{ij},v_{ij})$ the derivative of adjusted-curve (31), yet also requires every measure to be linear in
adjusted control points. Recomputing a normalized derivative from unknown adjusted controls makes (33) nonlinear. The
prototype freezes derivatives and quadrature arc lengths from the input curve, consistent with §3.1's fixed original
directions. This is an explicit project interpretation of that linearity requirement, not a quoted algorithm detail. It
approximates normal displacement, not exact closest-point distance or curvature preservation. Zero tangents are
unsupported and rejected.

Stored page 41 says to replace $(u,v)$ by $(1,0)$ to measure horizontal displacement. In (33) this selects $-\Delta Y$;
horizontal displacement requires $(0,1)$, up to overall sign. Preserve the printed source and flag this before extending
(7) to curves. This passage has not been compared against the author copy. The first prototype does not implement it.

### Coefficient count (26): derived correction, not an author-confirmed erratum

Stored page 33 and author page 33 (its (25)) both print

$$(N_V-2)^2+\left(N_V-\frac{N_V-1}{2}\right)=\frac32(N_V-2)(N_V-1).$$

The preceding Step 4 count is

$$\sum_{k=1}^{N_V-2}(N_V-k)=N_V(N_V-2)-\frac{(N_V-1)(N_V-2)}2.$$

Adding the Step 5 count $(N_V-2)^2$ therefore gives the project-derived correction

$$(N_V-2)^2+(N_V-2)\left(N_V-\frac{N_V-1}{2}\right)=\frac32(N_V-2)(N_V-1).$$

The source's $N_V=15$ example gives 104 + 169 = 273, consistent with this derivation. Both retrieved versions contain
the discrepancy; the final journal typesetting and any author erratum remain unverified. This is an encoding storage
count, not a fitting constraint, and does not block the prototype.

## Disposition

Transcription corruptions are corrected through strict regeneration patches. The version differences above are
**confirmed source discrepancies**; the original text is preserved and supported alternatives are labeled separately.
The width-weight behavior and derivative linearity interpretation are **pending model assessment**, not optical
acceptance. The prototype's geometric tests establish algebraic relationships only. Automatic feature recognition,
font-wide grouping, integer selection, topology guards and compatibility with the delivered raster remain separate
implementation and evaluation work.
<!-- cspell:words nullspace underdetermined CGAL Shene's Casteljau Forsgren nondegenerate linearization SLSQP nalgebra Ogita Oishi Mattingley autovectorization reassoc stationarity -->

## Completed diagonal-fit reuse experiment

The question is whether editing interactions can avoid repeating completed glyph fitting across renders. Following
[FreeType's memory-bounded glyph caches](https://freetype.org/freetype2/docs/reference/ft2-cache_subsystem.html), first
measure exact repeated fitting inputs during typing, layout/spacing changes, setting changes and revisits. The proposed
adaptation retains completed diagonal outcomes within an immutable loaded font, with bounded least-recently-used
storage. Key the complete original source geometry, upstream commands, reference anchors, size and native-axis ownership
by exact floating bits; a changed input always computes a fresh outcome. Unsupported outcomes can be reused, while
errors remain fresh. No approximate matching, geometry changes, fitting thresholds or glyph rules are included.

Keep request validation, scalar resolution, donor construction, rasterization, metrics, kerning and layout authoritative
on every call. Raw-byte entry points remain uncached. A full request-result cache and intermediate certificate cache are
outside this experiment. Compare the ordinary SIMD baseline with both cold and repeated interactions; count hits,
misses, eviction and retained payload separately from timing. Adoption requires useful interaction gains, controlled
cold overhead and unchanged delivery across request order, settings, eviction, errors and font lifetimes. Record the
census, identities, failures and browser evidence under `out/diagnostics/glyph-reuse-optimization/`; preserve published
preview selections and the approved comparison.

The completed-fit cache is retained after the interaction experiment. In both families, repeat/layout/spacing/kerning
and color changes repeat every default specimen fit; appending a new character repeats 28 of 29. The loaded-font cache
retains up to 2 MiB of key/command/reason payload and 256 entries, with bounded bookkeeping overhead. Full-key equality
authorizes reuse after a digest-assisted lookup. Detailed fit diagnostics were already discarded by this delivery caller
and are not retained; successful abstentions are cached while errors retry. Font destruction releases the cache.

All 563 delivery checks and 593 generator tests pass. Ordinary browser-worker interaction and confirmation batches show
about 88–91% lower warm render time for the default specimen, typically around 9 ms. New sizes and weights still compute
fresh geometry and incur a few percent overhead. Retained settings can be revisited cheaply, while evicted settings
recompute normally. These are worker-render results from scripted requests, not mounted UI latency: the editor's
existing 150 ms text debounce remains separate. The measured four-setting sequence retains about 1.1–1.3 MB per font.
Classification: unchanged delivered output within the verification scope, with no new optical acceptance. No publication
selection or fitting model changes.

## Selective solver arithmetic experiment

The question is whether local reassociation recovers useful rendering time while retaining the diagonal compensation
lost under global fast-math. The adaptation confines LLVM `reassoc` to a separate dot-product proposal kernel in the
least-squares solve. SVD construction, rank selection, compensated norms, geometric predicates, solver acceptance and
all other arithmetic remain strict. Neither finite-value assumptions nor approximate functions are enabled.

[Rump's matrix-product error analysis](https://www.tuhh.de/ti3/paper/rump/Ru14c.pdf) supports an order-independent
rounding bound. This prototype uses the more conservative standard gamma bound, outward-rounded maximum-magnitude
products and an additive underflow allowance. Non-finite inputs, an unbounded estimate, or a result whose sign is not
resolved by that bound trigger the original ordered arithmetic. This is a local arithmetic filter, not a proof of an
unchanged active set or final pixels. Existing strict feasibility and stationarity checks remain authoritative.

Use an isolated source copy and matched strict/selected compiler pipelines, with the ordinary standard-SIMD package as a
third control. Verify effective flag placement and protected compensated arithmetic, exercise cancellation and
exceptional operands, compare the complete delivery matrix, then time ordinary browser workers only after correctness
checks. No fitting thresholds, font-specific rules or published selection change. Retain source/package identities, all
failures and direct-app timing in `out/diagnostics/selective-math-optimization/`. Promotion requires a useful direct
gain and assessment of any delivered differences; mechanical parity alone does not establish optical quality.

The filtered projection prototype is declined at the performance gate. All 563 delivery checks match the ordinary app,
including the 288-cell matrix, default glyphs, general API controls and exports. Compiled-kernel probes retain the
compensation witness and satisfy the tested exact-rational error bounds. Twelve fresh browser sessions show essentially
no matched-pipeline gain: Roboto is 0.06% slower and Source Sans 0.31% faster. The complete experimental package is
17.96% and 10.22% slower than the ordinary SIMD app, respectively. Those direct differences include the compiler
pipeline and filtering overhead; they do not establish that reassociation itself causes that slowdown. This narrow
boundary preserves the tested output but supplies no practical adoption benefit. Broader kernels remain untested.

## Global fast-math experiment

The scoped question is whether broad fast-math changes delivered output or ordinary browser-worker rendering time
relative to standard SIMD. [LLVM fast-math flags](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#fast-math-flags) supply the
semantics: reassociation, approximate functions, reciprocal substitution, contraction, insignificant signed zeros and
assumptions that values are finite. This is a diagnostic experiment, not an assertion that the geometry satisfies those
assumptions.

The project adaptation processes a single merged Rust LLVM module through the same optimizer/code generator in strict
and fast modes, then retains the ordinary WASM link and bindings. The fast mode marks floating instructions before that
optimization; the strict control uses the same extra pipeline without those flags. Inspect input/output IR and an
arithmetic witness to confirm effective transformations. Compare the strict control with the maintained SIMD package
separately so a compiler-pipeline difference cannot be attributed to fast-math. Standard SIMD stays enabled on all
sides; dependency versions, geometric rules and publication scope stay fixed.

Capture output differences without stopping at the first changed glyph. Cover both families, ASCII, sizes, weights,
fitting/scanner modes, diagonals enabled/disabled, layout, metadata, errors and exports. Time fresh paired ordinary
browser workers with reversed order, identical-build controls and the established pangram/stress requests. Changed
output does not itself establish optical damage, and faster timing does not justify weakening numerical guarantees. No
main-app selection, deployment or optical acceptance is included. Detailed evidence belongs in
`out/diagnostics/fast-math-optimization/`.

The diagnostic build is not promoted. Fast-math removes a compensation term on a finite arithmetic witness and changes
pixels in 140 of 144 diagonal-enabled matrix cases, including 18 default-setting glyphs. All disabled matrix cases,
layout, metadata and general API controls match. The matched strict experimental build agrees with the app throughout
delivery comparisons, separating the observed output changes from compiler-pipeline effects. The user rejected the
visible result because it negates most diagonal compensation; the compensated-arithmetic invariant failure is also
confirmed.

Thirty-four fresh browser sessions show a direct fixed-pangram reduction of about 7.5% for Roboto and 8.9% for Source
Sans versus the maintained app, and about 10% on varied requests. The matched strict/fast comparison shows larger gains,
but its strict pipeline is slower than the app with diagonals enabled. Direct package comparisons therefore supplement
the causal arithmetic comparison; compiler-pipeline effects must not be described as fast-math gains. The timing scope
and all sessions, including identical-build controls, belong to the detailed report. Any future arithmetic adoption must
isolate a kernel and justify its numerical error contract; this experiment supplies no global safety guarantee or new
optical acceptance.

The requested visual review compares frozen maintained SIMD and experimental fast-math delivery packages. It captures

## Source discrepancies and interpretation

### Symmetry normal: supported alternative in the author copy

Stored page 22 defines the mean direction $D$ along matching segments, but its two displacement numerators use $D\cdot$
the positional mismatch. That measures tangential sliding rather than normal separation. The author copy, page 22,
explicitly uses $(D_y,-D_x)\cdot$ the mismatch for both endpoints (its subsequent equation is (15)). This agrees with
the normal-component construction in §3.1 and the curved symmetry expression on stored page 41. The stored transcription
retains $D\cdot$ faithfully; use the author-supported rotated normal when implementing this relationship. Reject a
zero-length mean direction rather than divide by zero. Symmetry fitting is outside the first prototype.

### Width mapping derivative: supported alternative in the author copy

Stored page 29 prints $\partial v/\partial w=\sqrt\theta$. Its own (22), $v=\frac23 w^{3/2}$, differentiates to
$\sqrt w$. The author copy, page 29, explicitly prints $\sqrt w$ before its (21). This also gives
$\Delta v\approx\sqrt w\,(\gamma_2/\sqrt w)=\gamma_2$, the stated local bucket correspondence. The stored transcription
retains $\sqrt\theta$; an implementation should use the verified mapping and its derivative. The mapping is only
approximate for finite rectangles: $u$ depends on $w$ as well as $\theta$.

### Width matching weight: surprising, but faithfully printed

Both copies, PDF page 23, print

$$\psi_1=\frac{500}{H^2}\exp\left[-\left(\frac{w_1-w_2}{0.7}\right)^2-\left(\frac{\Delta\theta}{9}\right)^2\right]$$

and explicitly say radians. No source here supports replacing 9 by degrees or another constant. At $\pi/2$ the
orientation factor is approximately 0.970, so this is a weak directional preference. The prototype keeps the printed
constant and reports this consequence. The 0.7 width scale also needs an explicit unit convention: unlike $H$-normalized
terms, it does not automatically rescale when input coordinate units change. The prototype uses pixel units and exposes
that width scale, without tuning it to glyph pixels.

### Curves: correspondence, fixed coefficients and a coordinate inconsistency

Stored page 40 and author page 40 both use **one third** as an example of mapping a point on a polygon segment to the
same fraction of its curve-parameter interval. This is correct and separate from the **midpoint** rule (32). For $k_i$
intervals the prototype uses $j=0,\ldots,k_i-1$.

The prose calls $(u_{ij},v_{ij})$ the derivative of adjusted-curve (31), yet also requires every measure to be linear in
adjusted control points. Recomputing a normalized derivative from unknown adjusted controls makes (33) nonlinear. The
prototype freezes derivatives and quadrature arc lengths from the input curve, consistent with §3.1's fixed original
directions. This is an explicit project interpretation of that linearity requirement, not a quoted algorithm detail. It
approximates normal displacement, not exact closest-point distance or curvature preservation. Zero tangents are
unsupported and rejected.

Stored page 41 says to replace $(u,v)$ by $(1,0)$ to measure horizontal displacement. In (33) this selects $-\Delta Y$;
horizontal displacement requires $(0,1)$, up to overall sign. Preserve the printed source and flag this before extending
(7) to curves. This passage has not been compared against the author copy. The first prototype does not implement it.

### Coefficient count (26): derived correction, not an author-confirmed erratum

Stored page 33 and author page 33 (its (25)) both print

$$(N_V-2)^2+\left(N_V-\frac{N_V-1}{2}\right)=\frac32(N_V-2)(N_V-1).$$

The preceding Step 4 count is

$$\sum_{k=1}^{N_V-2}(N_V-k)=N_V(N_V-2)-\frac{(N_V-1)(N_V-2)}2.$$

Adding the Step 5 count $(N_V-2)^2$ therefore gives the project-derived correction

$$(N_V-2)^2+(N_V-2)\left(N_V-\frac{N_V-1}{2}\right)=\frac32(N_V-2)(N_V-1).$$

The source's $N_V=15$ example gives 104 + 169 = 273, consistent with this derivation. Both retrieved versions contain
the discrepancy; the final journal typesetting and any author erratum remain unverified. This is an encoding storage
count, not a fitting constraint, and does not block the prototype.

## Disposition

Transcription corruptions are corrected through strict regeneration patches. The version differences above are
**confirmed source discrepancies**; the original text is preserved and supported alternatives are labeled separately.
The width-weight behavior and derivative linearity interpretation are **pending model assessment**, not optical
acceptance. The prototype's geometric tests establish algebraic relationships only. Automatic feature recognition,
font-wide grouping, integer selection, topology guards and compatibility with the delivered raster remain separate
implementation and evaluation work.

## Completed diagonal-fit reuse experiment

The question is whether editing interactions can avoid repeating completed glyph fitting across renders. Following
[FreeType's memory-bounded glyph caches](https://freetype.org/freetype2/docs/reference/ft2-cache_subsystem.html), first
measure exact repeated fitting inputs during typing, layout/spacing changes, setting changes and revisits. The proposed

## Source model and adaptation

The coordinate unknowns are displacements of source endpoints and cubic controls at nominal scale one. All feature
correspondences and normals remain fixed coefficients. A `Sample` is a supplied affine combination of those controls;
its cubic constructor uses the Bernstein weights from (31). A shared vertex has one pair of unknowns, including when
several features refer to it.

| Prototype operation      | Source and relationship                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| ------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `edge`                   | (1) integrates squared normal displacement exactly for a straight segment; (2),(3) penalize relative stretching and bending in its original frame.                                                                                                                                                               |
| `pair`, `preserve_width` | (4),(5) use twice the supplied medial radius and signed projected relative width error. Ink and white-space features are explicit inputs, as in §3.2. The midpoint default is only for constructed synthetic contacts.                                                                                           |
| `match_width`            | (17) couples changes relative to source widths, preserving intended contrast rather than forcing identical widths. Caller supplies eligible feature pairs; mixed ink/white matching is unsupported.                                                                                                              |
| `offset`                 | (11)–(13) evaluate caller-supplied signed integer offsets with the finite printed weights. Their components remain in the absolute pixel grid. No rounding or offset search occurs.                                                                                                                              |
| `curve`                  | (31)–(33) sample normal displacement at parameter midpoints; source tangents and midpoint-speed arc weights are frozen.                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| `solve`                  | Continuous least squares with caller-frozen controls eliminated. [NumPy `lstsq`](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.linalg.lstsq.html) supplies a minimum-displacement-norm solution when the system is deficient; rank is reported. This does not implement Hobby's integer/lattice solver. |

**Project adaptation for curve shape:** apply (2),(3)'s stretching/bending construction to the cubic derivative at each
sample. With original derivative $q'$, derivative displacement $\delta q'$, speed $s=\|q'\|$ and midpoint arc weight
$\Delta\ell=s/k$, the residuals are

$$\sqrt{\alpha_2\Delta\ell}\frac{q'\cdot\delta q'}{s^2},\qquad
\sqrt{\alpha_3\Delta\ell}\frac{(q'_y,-q'_x)\cdot\delta q'}{s^2}.$$

This follows the local relative-strain construction of (2),(3) and §6's linear control-point representation. It is not a
verbatim formula from the report, an exact curvature constraint or a nonlinear closest-point calculation. It reduces to
the original edge measures for a linear cubic. The supplied examples use 16 midpoint intervals; a convergence test
checks the quadrature separately. Automatic adaptive subdivision and medial-axis extraction are outside this tool. Using
$25/H$ for both derivative measures transfers the straight-edge weights as a project hypothesis; the report does not
independently establish their balance against curved-stroke width changes. The normal sign differs between `edge` and
`curve`, following their source expressions; it is inert for those squared shape terms. Offset signs remain fixed.

The normal-only curve negative control remains in the JSON: it demonstrates why (33) alone is insufficient for this
experiment. The concentric cubic correspondences are supplied radial approximations, not claimed exact medial contacts
on arbitrary curves. Positive projected sampled widths do not prove the whole curves remain valid or nested.

The source weight $\psi_1$ retains its printed denominator **9 radians**, giving a 90°/parallel weight ratio of about
0.970. Its width difference scale is explicitly 0.7 pixels. Changing coordinate units requires changing this scale and
$H$ together; geometric unit-rescaling tests do so. Integer targets and the absolute pixel grid intentionally break
arbitrary rotation and size invariance. The rotated examples use integer offsets supplied in each example's absolute
grid, not rotated fractional offsets.

## Experiments and findings

The deterministic examples use the source's suggested weights, $H=14$, and supplied targets. They are algebraic
experiments, not font-specific fitting policies or optical acceptance:

- Two straight stems: one supplied offset and a coupled width-change measure move both stems, including at 30° and 45°.
  At 0°, the source widths 1.265625 become approximately 1.000015 and 1.040643. Finite penalties permit residual error;
  the second stem has no independently supplied integer target. Arbitrary-angle projection can also increase width.
- Curved paired borders: the derivative-shape adaptation limits maximum control movement to about 0.189 px, compared
  with 39.714 px for the normal-only negative control. This demonstrates missing shape control in the incomplete model,
  not proof of safe general curve fitting. Both achieve approximately 0.97950 px at the constrained sample, from 1.26588
  px. The sampled widths still vary appreciably near the supplied target.
- Square ring: both supplied ink widths become approximately 1.000008 px while the white feature grows from 3.6 to
  3.756027 px. The counter stays open in this construction; no general counter-preservation guarantee follows.
- A shared T-junction fixture keeps its caller-frozen vertex exact while adjacent geometry moves. A completely frozen
  incompatible width reports nonzero offset residuals. The solver does not label that outcome successful fitting.

Tests cover the exact displacement integral, stretching/bending, relative contrast, radius versus chord, coupled width
response, geometric translations/rotations/unit changes, fixed-grid projection, curved shape and quadrature, supplied
counter relationships, frozen junctions and invalid inputs. There is no automatic feature ownership, movement bound,
self-intersection check, topology guard, fallback policy or source-font corpus comparison yet. Residuals are evidence
per constraint group, not a quality or acceptance score.
# mutator

Mutation testing for Clojure, Java, Go, TypeScript, Rust, and Python. One run detects the language of each source file, applies that language's mutation rules, and writes the snapshot [uml-viewer](https://github.com/unclebob/uml-viewer) already reads.

Clojure follows [clj-mutate](https://github.com/unclebob/clj-mutate). Go follows [mutate4go](https://github.com/unclebob/mutate4go). Java follows [mutate4java](https://github.com/unclebob/mutate4java). TypeScript, Rust, and Python use the same decisions as Java, spelled in that language. Function names and namespaces come from [crapper](https://github.com/unclebob/crapper), which is what uml-viewer joins to `.metrics/crap.edn`.

A mutant is killed when the tests fail or time out. It survives when the tests still pass. A site on a line the coverage report does not hit is uncovered and is not run. The score uml-viewer paints is killed / (killed + survived).

## Run

```bash
./mutator
```

The first run creates `.venv` and installs the tool. crapper has to be checked out next to this directory (`../crapper`), because that is where the namespace and function names come from. From a project root the tool walks the tree, skips `test`, `spec`, `vendor`, `node_modules`, and `target`, and writes `.metrics/mutate/<namespace>.edn`.

The first run of a tree executes every covered mutant. Start with the file you are working on.

```bash
./mutator src/demo/core.clj          # one file, or a directory
./mutator --scan src/demo           # list sites, do not run tests
./mutator --changed                 # git additions and edits
./mutator --mutate-all              # rerun killed mutants too
./mutator --no-coverage             # do not skip uncovered lines
./mutator --use-existing-coverage   # read reports already on disk
./mutator --test-command "pytest -q tests/test_demo.py"
./mutator --max-workers 3 src/demo/core.clj
```

Once a snapshot exists, the next run is differential. It reruns survivors and every site in a function whose text changed. Killed mutants in an unchanged function stay killed. `--since-last-run` is that same selection. `--mutate-all` ignores it.

Exit `0` when every executed mutant was killed. Exit `2` when the baseline tests fail. Exit `3` when a mutant survives. A failed baseline does not rewrite the snapshot.

## Workers

Mutants of one file run at the same time. The default is one worker per core. `--max-workers` sets the cap. The run uses the smaller of that cap, the number of cores, and the number of selected sites. Files are still taken one at a time.

Each worker is a directory under `target/mutation-workers`. The file being mutated is a private copy. A module that reaches that file through a relative import is copied too, so Node resolves the import to the private copy. The rest of the tree is linked. The original files stay as they are. The overlay is removed when that file's mutants finish.

Projects with a root Vite or Vitest configuration keep project inputs private in
each worker, including setup files and glob assets. In Git projects this covers
tracked and non-ignored untracked files; other projects copy local files except
dependencies and build outputs. Dependencies remain linked. This preserves
worker-local aliases and file URLs without changing the project's configuration.
The optional integration regression uses an existing installation:
`MUTATOR_VITEST_NODE_MODULES=/path/to/node_modules .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/test_engine.py -k vitest_worker`.

The baseline still runs once, in the real tree, before any worker starts. The mutant command then runs inside the worker, in the same directory it would have used in the real tree, so a relative path such as `src` or `./pkg` refers to the overlay. A copy left under `target/mutator-backup/` by an interrupted older run is restored before a non-scan run.

## Snapshot

uml-viewer loads every `*.edn` file under `.metrics/mutate`. Each file is one namespace. A Java file with an inner class, or a Go file with a function and a method, therefore writes more than one file. Two Go files in the same package share one snapshot, and rerunning one of them keeps the other's forms.

```clojure
{:version 1
 :source "src/demo/board.py"
 :namespace "demo.board.Board"
 :outcomes {"[\"src/demo/board.py\",\"demo.board.Board\",\"defn/place\",10,11,\">\",\">=\"]" :survived}
 :forms [{:id "defn/place"
          :kind "defn"
          :file "src/demo/board.py"
          :line 2
          :end-line 4
          :hash "…"
          :killed 1
          :survived 1
          :uncovered 0
          :sites 2}
         {:id "defn-/_hide"
          :kind "defn-"
          :killed 0
          :survived 0
          :uncovered 1
          :sites 1}]}
```

`:namespace` is the class key crapper uses. The form id is what the viewer splits:

| Form id | Operation | Private |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `defn/place` | `place` | no |
| `defn-/hide` | `hide` | yes |

`:sites` is every mutation in the function, including uncovered ones. The viewer prints `---no mutation sites---` when that count is zero.

| Language | `:namespace` | `:name` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Clojure | the `ns` | the `defn` / `defn-` name |
| Java | `package.Class`, or `package.Outer.Inner` | the method name |
| Go | the package import path, or `import/path.Receiver` | the function or method name |
| TypeScript | the dotted module path, or `module.Class` | the function or method name |
| Rust | `crate::module`, or `crate::module::Type` | the function or method name |
| Python | the dotted module path, or `module.Class` | the function or method name |

`defn-` is Clojure's private form. Elsewhere a private method, an unexported Go function, a Python name that starts with `_`, a Rust function that is not `pub`, or a TypeScript `private` / `#` name uses `defn-/`.

## What each language mutates

Tokens inside strings, comments, and quoted Clojure forms are left alone. A replacement that does not compile fails the test run and counts as killed.

| Language | Mutations |
| --- | --- |
| Clojure | clj-mutate's head symbols: `+`/`-`, `*` to `/`, `inc`/`dec`, comparisons, `=`/`not=`, `if`/`if-not`, `when`/`when-not`, `and`/`or`, and the seq, predicate, and coercion pairs. `true`/`false` and `0`/`1` anywhere. |
| Java | `true`/`false`, `==`/`!=`, `<`/`<=`, `>`/`>=`, `+`/`-`, `*`/`/`, `&&`/`||`, delete `!` and unary `-`, `0`/`1`. Constructors are not entries, matching crapper. |
| Go | mutate4go: `+`/`-`, `*` to `/` only, comparisons, `==`/`!=`, `true`/`false`, `&&`/`||`, `0`/`1`. |
| TypeScript | the Java set, plus `===`/`!==`, `??` to `||`, and `?.` to `.`. A call or index drops `?.` (`a?.()` becomes `a()`). `.js`, `.jsx`, `.mjs`, and `.cjs` use these rules. |
| Rust | the Java set (`&&`/`||`, `!`, unary `-`). |
| Python | the Java set, spelled `and`/`or`, `not`, and `True`/`False`. |

## Tests and coverage

The baseline command has to pass before any mutant runs. A mutant's timeout is ten times that baseline, and at least two seconds. `--timeout-factor` changes the multiple. `--test-command` replaces the default. Defaults:

| Language | Command | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Clojure | `clj -M:spec --tag ~no-mutate` when Speclj is on the classpath, otherwise `clj -M:test` or `bb spec` | nearest `deps.edn` or `bb.edn` |
| Java | `mvn -q test -DexcludeTags=no-mutate` | nearest `pom.xml` |
| Go | `go test -count=1` of the file's package | nearest `go.mod` |
| TypeScript | `npm test` | nearest `package.json` |
| Rust | `cargo test` | nearest `Cargo.toml` |
| Python | the project's `.venv` or `venv` Python running `pytest`, or `unittest discover` | nearest project file |

Coverage is generated with crapper's commands unless `--use-existing-coverage` or `--no-coverage` is set. A file missing from the report is treated as uncovered, and the run says so.

## Development

python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install -e '.[dev]'
.venv/bin/pytest

# mutator

Mutation testing for Clojure, Java, Go, TypeScript, Rust, and Python. One run detects the language of each source file, applies that language's mutation rules, and writes the snapshot [uml-viewer](https://github.com/unclebob/uml-viewer) already reads.

Clojure follows [clj-mutate](https://github.com/unclebob/clj-mutate). Go follows [mutate4go](https://github.com/unclebob/mutate4go). Java follows [mutate4java](https://github.com/unclebob/mutate4java). TypeScript, Rust, and Python use the same decisions as Java, spelled in that language. Function names and namespaces come from [crapper](https://github.com/unclebob/crapper), which is what uml-viewer joins to `.metrics/crap.edn`.

A mutant is killed when the tests fail or time out. It survives when the tests still pass. A site on a line the coverage report does not hit is uncovered and is not run. The score uml-viewer paints is killed / (killed + survived).

## Run

```bash
./mutator
```

The first run creates `.venv` and installs the tool. crapper has to be checked out next to this directory (`../crapper`), because that is where the namespace and function names come from. From a project root the tool walks the tree, skips `test`, `spec`, `vendor`, `node_modules`, and `target`, and writes `.metrics/mutate/<namespace>.edn`.

The first run of a tree executes every covered mutant. Start with the file you are working on.

```bash
./mutator src/demo/core.clj          # one file, or a directory
./mutator --scan src/demo           # list sites, do not run tests
./mutator --changed                 # git additions and edits
./mutator --mutate-all              # rerun killed mutants too
./mutator --no-coverage             # do not skip uncovered lines
./mutator --use-existing-coverage   # read reports already on disk
./mutator --test-command "pytest -q tests/test_demo.py"
./mutator --max-workers 3 src/demo/core.clj
```

Once a snapshot exists, the next run is differential. It reruns survivors and every site in a function whose text changed. Killed mutants in an unchanged function stay killed. `--since-last-run` is that same selection. `--mutate-all` ignores it.

Exit `0` when every executed mutant was killed. Exit `2` when the baseline tests fail. Exit `3` when a mutant survives. A failed baseline does not rewrite the snapshot.

## Workers

Mutants of one file run at the same time. The default is one worker per core. `--max-workers` sets the cap. The run uses the smaller of that cap, the number of cores, and the number of selected sites. Files are still taken one at a time.

Each worker is a directory under `target/mutation-workers`. The file being mutated is a private copy. A module that reaches that file through a relative import is copied too, so Node resolves the import to the private copy. The rest of the tree is linked. The original files stay as they are. The overlay is removed when that file's mutants finish.

Projects with a root Vite or Vitest configuration keep project inputs private in
each worker, including setup files and glob assets. In Git projects this covers
tracked and non-ignored untracked files; other projects copy local files except
dependencies and build outputs. Dependencies remain linked. This preserves
worker-local aliases and file URLs without changing the project's configuration.
The optional integration regression uses an existing installation:
`MUTATOR_VITEST_NODE_MODULES=/path/to/node_modules .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/test_engine.py -k vitest_worker`.

The baseline still runs once, in the real tree, before any worker starts. The mutant command then runs inside the worker, in the same directory it would have used in the real tree, so a relative path such as `src` or `./pkg` refers to the overlay. A copy left under `target/mutator-backup/` by an interrupted older run is restored before a non-scan run.

## Snapshot

uml-viewer loads every `*.edn` file under `.metrics/mutate`. Each file is one namespace. A Java file with an inner class, or a Go file with a function and a method, therefore writes more than one file. Two Go files in the same package share one snapshot, and rerunning one of them keeps the other's forms.

```clojure
{:version 1
 :source "src/demo/board.py"
 :namespace "demo.board.Board"
 :outcomes {"[\"src/demo/board.py\",\"demo.board.Board\",\"defn/place\",10,11,\">\",\">=\"]" :survived}
 :forms [{:id "defn/place"
          :kind "defn"
          :file "src/demo/board.py"
          :line 2
          :end-line 4
          :hash "…"
          :killed 1
          :survived 1
          :uncovered 0
          :sites 2}
         {:id "defn-/_hide"
          :kind "defn-"
          :killed 0
          :survived 0
          :uncovered 1
          :sites 1}]}
```

`:namespace` is the class key crapper uses. The form id is what the viewer splits:

| Form id | Operation | Private |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `defn/place` | `place` | no |
| `defn-/hide` | `hide` | yes |

`:sites` is every mutation in the function, including uncovered ones. The viewer prints `---no mutation sites---` when that count is zero.

| Language | `:namespace` | `:name` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Clojure | the `ns` | the `defn` / `defn-` name |
| Java | `package.Class`, or `package.Outer.Inner` | the method name |
| Go | the package import path, or `import/path.Receiver` | the function or method name |
| TypeScript | the dotted module path, or `module.Class` | the function or method name |
| Rust | `crate::module`, or `crate::module::Type` | the function or method name |
| Python | the dotted module path, or `module.Class` | the function or method name |

`defn-` is Clojure's private form. Elsewhere a private method, an unexported Go function, a Python name that starts with `_`, a Rust function that is not `pub`, or a TypeScript `private` / `#` name uses `defn-/`.

## What each language mutates

Tokens inside strings, comments, and quoted Clojure forms are left alone. A replacement that does not compile fails the test run and counts as killed.

| Language | Mutations |
| --- | --- |
| Clojure | clj-mutate's head symbols: `+`/`-`, `*` to `/`, `inc`/`dec`, comparisons, `=`/`not=`, `if`/`if-not`, `when`/`when-not`, `and`/`or`, and the seq, predicate, and coercion pairs. `true`/`false` and `0`/`1` anywhere. |
| Java | `true`/`false`, `==`/`!=`, `<`/`<=`, `>`/`>=`, `+`/`-`, `*`/`/`, `&&`/`||`, delete `!` and unary `-`, `0`/`1`. Constructors are not entries, matching crapper. |
| Go | mutate4go: `+`/`-`, `*` to `/` only, comparisons, `==`/`!=`, `true`/`false`, `&&`/`||`, `0`/`1`. |
| TypeScript | the Java set, plus `===`/`!==`, `??` to `||`, and `?.` to `.`. A call or index drops `?.` (`a?.()` becomes `a()`). `.js`, `.jsx`, `.mjs`, and `.cjs` use these rules. |
| Rust | the Java set (`&&`/`||`, `!`, unary `-`). |
| Python | the Java set, spelled `and`/`or`, `not`, and `True`/`False`. |

## Tests and coverage

The baseline command has to pass before any mutant runs. A mutant's timeout is ten times that baseline, and at least two seconds. `--timeout-factor` changes the multiple. `--test-command` replaces the default. Defaults:

| Language | Command | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Clojure | `clj -M:spec --tag ~no-mutate` when Speclj is on the classpath, otherwise `clj -M:test` or `bb spec` | nearest `deps.edn` or `bb.edn` |
| Java | `mvn -q test -DexcludeTags=no-mutate` | nearest `pom.xml` |
| Go | `go test -count=1` of the file's package | nearest `go.mod` |
| TypeScript | `npm test` | nearest `package.json` |
| Rust | `cargo test` | nearest `Cargo.toml` |
| Python | the project's `.venv` or `venv` Python running `pytest`, or `unittest discover` | nearest project file |

Coverage is generated with crapper's commands unless `--use-existing-coverage` or `--no-coverage` is set. A file missing from the report is treated as uncovered, and the run says so.

        key = (site.namespace, site.form_id)

    if cache_key in baselines:

    baseline = runner.run(command, cwd, None)
    if baseline.code != 0:

        baselines[cache_key] = (False, baseline.seconds, tail)

    message = f"Baseline failed for {file_key}: {display_command(command)}"
    if tail:
        message = f"{message}\n{tail}"
    return RunResult(path=file_key, forms=[], written=[], baseline_failed=True, baseline_message=message)


def _apply_selected(
    path,
    root,
    original,
    selected,
    runner,
    language,
    test_command,
    timeout_factor,
    file_key,
    baselines,
    outcomes,
    max_workers,
) -> RunResult | None:
    if not selected:
        return None
    command, cwd = test_plan(root, path, language, test_command)
    cache_key = (_command_key(command), str(cwd))
    _remember_baseline(baselines, cache_key, runner, command, cwd)
    ok, seconds, tail = baselines[cache_key]
    if not ok:
        return _baseline_failure(file_key, command, tail)
    timeout = max(2.0, seconds * timeout_factor)
    run_mutants(
        root,
        path,
        original,
        selected,
        max_workers,
        runner,
        command,
        cwd,

        file_key,

## Final verdict: new tests faithfully pin existing behavior — no blocking findings

Read the five new cases plus `project_correspondence` helper at the end of [rows.rs:115-303](/Users/dimitri/Documents/Code/personal/Inkplate/font_generator/tools/generator/src/diagonal_fitting/rows.rs). Prior baseline-equivalence verdict stands: production hashes for `mod.rs`/`crossing.rs` in `review-source-final.json` are unchanged (`bfb334…`, `b03dc5…`); only `rows.rs` changed by tests and comment pruning.

- **Helper ([rows.rs:115-135](tools/generator/src/diagonal_fitting/rows.rs)) is faithful.** It replicates the `System`-style projector (`=` then `-=`, via real `basis_row`). Correct for these tests: the `edge` oblique case asserts dot products (insensitive to the `=`/`+=` signed-zero split), and the `pair` cases assert accept/reject, `width`, and finiteness — never zero-slot bits. No new behavior invented.
- **Oblique edge ([rows.rs:226-244](tools/generator/src/diagonal_fitting/rows.rs)):** 3-4-5 edge gives `length=5`, `alpha1=1`, checks `sum·d=√(5/4)`, `diff·d=-√(5/12)`, `stretch`/`bend` dots equal `√12.5/5`. Hand-verified against the guarded algebra. Pins the `/4` vs `/12` scales, `ri±rj` orientation, and tangent/normal selection the axis test cannot distinguish.
- **Coincident contacts ([rows.rs:247-253](tools/generator/src/diagonal_fitting/rows.rs)):** single-point geometry with positive equal radii (`width=other=3`) isolates the chord guard (`distance=0` → `Err`) before any projection. Faithful.
- **Zero first radius ([rows.rs:256-263](tools/generator/src/diagonal_fitting/rows.rs)):** `width=0` with tiny positive chord isolates the `width > 0` guard. Faithful.
- **Absolute-tolerance boundary ([rows.rs:266-283](tools/generator/src/diagonal_fitting/rows.rs)):** `width-other=1e-12` against bound `1e-12+0` pins strict `>` vs `>=`. Comment's exactness claim holds on the passing toolchain (`2*5e-13` exact by scaling; suite passes). Minor robustness note only: the `assert_eq!(width, 1e-12)` bit-exact check on a decimal-derived double is toolchain-sensitive, but it passed and guards the intended boundary; not a blocker.
- **Relative tolerance ([rows.rs:286-303](tools/generator/src/diagonal_fitting/rows.rs)):** mismatch `1e-10` exceeds the absolute term (`1e-12`, asserted) but passes via `1e-10*|other|` (`2.01e-10` bound). Isolates the relative term. Faithful.

No concrete test issue. The five valid survivors are addressed by tests that restate, not extend, the existing guards and Hobby scales.

# Working in this repository

Read the documents relevant to the task before making changes. Follow their linked contracts when the work crosses
component boundaries.

Before tackling a problem, follow the [research workflow](docs/evaluation.md#research-before-implementation).

- Use sourced, general geometric models; do not tune individual glyphs for pixel gains.
- Classify findings before requesting review or publishing; tests do not establish optical acceptance.
- Preserve the agreed preview scope and separate approved baseline.
- Use the shared shadcn Tooltip component for web tooltips instead of native `title` attributes.
- Keep rules and current state in their owner documents; link rather than duplicate.
- Keep contracts and READMEs concise. Apply this test to every contract statement: if changing it would break another
  component or an external consumer of its inputs, outputs, published formats, routes, forwarded requests, or build
  outcomes, it belongs; if only a person viewing the page would notice, it belongs in code and tests, not the contract.
  That excludes presentation, layout, display modes, control behavior, and formats produced and consumed inside one
  component. READMEs state setup, commands, and configuration only. Do not record implementation mechanics or change
  history in either; link to owner documents rather than restating their rules.

## Code placement

Maintained commands, apps and runtime live in `tools/`; exploratory prototypes, harnesses and adapters live in
`experiments/`. Read [experiment guidance](experiments/AGENTS.md) before adding or moving experiment code. Extend the
owning component rather than creating a parallel helper project. Maintained components never depend on `experiments/`;
experiments may use maintained APIs. Extract shared code only for concrete consumers. Record adoption of an experiment
in the owning design or iteration document, with the verification and interfaces that adoption requires.

## Task guidance

Read first, according to the task:

- Fitting, spacing, raster changes or evaluation tests: [evaluation rules](docs/evaluation.md).
- Renderer routing, settings or native layout: [generator API](tools/generator/API.md).
- Preview generation, comparison or publication: [generator contract](tools/generator/CONTRACT.md) and
  [review rules](docs/evaluation.md#review-and-decision).
- Web boundaries or publication: [web contract](tools/web/CONTRACT.md); setup and commands in the
  [web README](tools/web/README.md).
- WASM interface or build: [WASM README](tools/wasm/README.md).
- Experiments, prototypes or harnesses: [experiment guidance](experiments/AGENTS.md).
- Iteration scope, decisions or closure: [revision guide](docs/revisions/README.md) and the relevant revision index.
- Formatting and checks: [task recipes](justfile) and [hook configuration](lefthook.yml).
- Commit messages: [commit rules](commitlint.config.ts) and [allowed scopes](commit-scopes.json).

For model work, use the [revision guide](docs/revisions/README.md) to locate the relevant revision index and affected
iteration document before changing behavior. Revision indexes own approved/candidate identities; configuration and
policy files own the published preview selections.
